title: ADDF Light Games — Documentation Wiki
body: ## ADDF Light Games — Documentation Wiki **Edition:** ADDF Light Games · **Branch:** `ADDF_light_games` · **Status:** Stage 7 candidate, awaiting human review **Document authority:** [Framework specifications](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/FRAMEWORK_SPEC.md), [Project File Contracts](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/PROJECT_FILE_CONTRACTS.md), [Sprint Contracts](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/SPRINT_FILE_CONTRACTS.md) This is the **canonical Markdown wiki** for the game-development-focused Light edition of the Autonomous Duck Deployment Framework. It contains thorough reference material while the actual user experience begins with six project files and one consequential question at a time. **Start quickly:** [Root Quick Start](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/QUICK_START.md) · [Your First Session](#wiki-guides--first-session) · [Install Starter Kit](#wiki-guides--install) **Compare editions:** [Original ADDF vs. ADDF Light Games](#wiki-foundations--comparison) — full side-by-side table of philosophy, lifecycles, files, permission gates, onboarding, and recommended use cases. **One complete document:** [Generated MANUAL.md](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/MANUAL.md) — all chapters below, built from these wiki pages; do not edit it manually. ### Wiki navigation #### Foundations - [Overview](#wiki-foundations--overview) - [Philosophy](#wiki-foundations--philosophy) - [Original ADDF vs. ADDF Light Games](#wiki-foundations--comparison) - [Core Concepts](#wiki-foundations--core-concepts) - [Design](#wiki-lifecycle--design) - [Implement](#wiki-lifecycle--implement) - [Refine](#wiki-lifecycle--refine) - [Acceptance](#wiki-lifecycle--acceptance) #### Sprint workflow - [Overview](#wiki-sprints--overview) - [Backlog](#wiki-sprints--backlog) - [Planning](#wiki-sprints--planning) - [Approvals](#wiki-sprints--approvals) - [Review](#wiki-sprints--review) #### Guided learning - [Guided Discovery](#wiki-learning--guided-discovery) - [Checkpoints](#wiki-learning--checkpoints) - [Decisions](#wiki-learning--decisions) #### Agents and integrations - [Operating Contract](#wiki-agents--operating-contract) - [Permissions](#wiki-agents--permissions) - [Handoff](#wiki-agents--handoff) - [Claude Code](#wiki-agents--claude-code) - [Codex](#wiki-agents--codex) - [Openclaw](#wiki-agents--openclaw) #### Quality and safety - [Testing](#wiki-quality--testing) - [Playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting) - [Validation](#wiki-quality--validation) - [Failure Recovery](#wiki-quality--failure-recovery) - [Security](#wiki-quality--security) #### Reference - [File Reference](#wiki-reference--file-reference) - [Prompt Catalog](#wiki-reference--prompt-catalog) - [Troubleshooting](#wiki-reference--troubleshooting) - [Faq](#wiki-reference--faq) ### How to use this wiki Begin with the [Quick Start](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/QUICK_START.md) or the [first-session guide](#wiki-guides--first-session). You do **not** need to read every chapter before starting a game. During actual work, use the [Quick Reference](#wiki-guides--quick-reference) and read only the relevant stage's page. If you are a framework maintainer or educator, the full wiki covers the human design/learning process, approval safeguards, file contracts, optional agent integrations, testing, security, and recovery. The generated manual combines the pages without creating a competing source of truth. ### What is normative versus explanatory? - **Normative framework rules:** Approved `spec/` files. This wiki explains and illustrates them; it does not silently change their permissions. - **Project state:** A user's own `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GAME.md`, `STATE.md`, `DECISIONS.md` and sprint records. - **Canonical documentation prose:** `docs/light-games/**/*.md`, ordered by `manifest.txt`. - **Derived artifact:** Root `MANUAL.md` produced by `scripts/build_light_manual.py`; CI detects drift. - **Not yet finished:** Stage 8 branding/logo, Stage 9 website distribution, Stage 10 release packaging. The Stage 5 live Claude Code/Codex/OpenClaw runs remain openly unverified. ### Boundaries Original full ADDF documentation under `docs/` and `main` has not been replaced. The Light wiki is isolated under `docs/light-games/` to prevent conflicts, and its release must never auto-merge into or deploy over the original ADDF site. This wiki is distributed as Markdown under the repository's existing license; see the repository's [LICENSE](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/LICENSE) for exact terms. Links to vendor documentation are informational and may change with host versions.

title: What Is ADDF Light Games?
body: ## What Is ADDF Light Games? ADDF Light Games is a **human-guided, file-first AI game-development methodology**. It helps someone go from “I want to make a game” to a testable playable slice without requiring a complete game design document, a specific game engine, or an autonomous agent platform. The short loop is **Research → Design / Ideation → Implement → Refine → Acceptance**. It repeats for each bounded sprint. Research reveals uncertainty; Design chooses a viable experience; Implement produces approved changes; Refine responds to evidence; Acceptance belongs to the person playing or evaluating the result. ### When to use Use Light for solo developers, game-design students, prototypes, interaction designers, small teams, and developers learning from AI assistance. The first supported domain is **games and interactive playable experiences**, not a general replacement for original ADDF's broader software-development governance. The methodology works through a plain chat assistant and Markdown. A coding agent is optional for early discovery but valuable after you approve a technical plan. Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw are optional adapters, **not requirements**. ### What “Light” means Light describes the **user's operational workload**, not less rigorous permissions or shallow explanations. The documentation may be exhaustive while the runtime starts with **six files** and only adds the three-file sprint pack when a milestone exists. The agent researches, teaches relevant tradeoffs, drafts documentation, proposes actions and records actual results. The person decides consequential design direction, authorizes precise implementation scope and judges the playable outcome. You should spend your attention on **what the player does and what you learn from testing**, not on manually writing a dozen administrative files. ### The two repositories The **framework distribution** lives in the `ADDF_light_games` Git branch. It contains specifications, starter templates, prompts, optional integrations, examples, validators and this wiki. Your **game repository** is separate. The six starter files copied into it refer to that game. Never copy the framework's inherited root `AGENTS.md` into your game: that file belongs to the original full ADDF edition. ### The three non-negotiable gates | Gate | Human decides | Durable record | | --- | --- | --- | | **D — Design** | Meaningful design alternatives and the sprint's intended outcome | `DECISIONS.md` and `SPRINT.md` | | **I — Implementation** | Exact files, commands, dependencies, side effects and plan revision | `PLAN.md` | | **A — Acceptance** | Whether first-hand playtesting/review meets the sprint goal | `REVIEW.md` | A conversational “sounds good” about a concept **is not** permission to change code. A passing test **is not** player acceptance. ### What a first result looks like A user chooses a tiny dodge game. The agent compares direct versus accelerating movement, the person selects a style, and the agent drafts one sprint: move a placeholder duck in an arena and avoid one repeating obstacle. The agent shows exactly what it plans to change and asks for authorization. After implementation, the person plays, observes a readability problem and requests a small refinement. The sprint ends only with the person's verdict. This is more useful than generating an entire untested game from one sentence. ### Common failures **Too much process:** Require the full wiki before starting, or make the user fill every field. Instead, start with one question and let the agent draft files. **Too little control:** Skip the dry-run approval for “obvious” changes. Instead, use a short exact plan. **False progress:** Treat an AI's claim that a build works as evidence of gameplay feel. Instead, distinguish verified command output from a human observation. ### Related [Philosophy](#wiki-foundations--philosophy) · [Original ADDF comparison](#wiki-foundations--comparison) · [Quick Start guide](#wiki-guides--first-session) · [Glossary](#wiki-foundations--glossary)

title: Philosophy: Deep Reference, Small Runtime
body: ## Philosophy: Deep Reference, Small Runtime ADDF Light Games retains original ADDF's **file-first memory, bounded roles and human approval** while reducing the number of documents and repetitive prompts needed to run an ordinary game-design sprint. ### When to use Read this when deciding whether the framework is too heavy, when explaining it to a class or team, or when considering a new rule that would add friction to a beginner's first session. ### Principle 1 — The human designs the experience The agent can research camera options, prototype a movement controller and summarize playtest comments. It must not silently decide whether the game should be a puzzle or a shooter, whether acceleration is desirable, or whether a playable slice “feels good.” Those are meaningful human choices informed by evidence. Not every variable name is a vote. **T0 routine** implementation details can be resolved by the agent inside an approved plan. **T1 significant** choices require a design decision. **T2 high-impact** matters—security, costs, destructive actions, public publishing—require stricter review and possibly separate special authorization. ### Principle 2 — Learning is part of making An agent should explain *why* the first sprint tests movement or feedback, not merely provide code. A learning checkpoint may ask the designer to predict whether instant movement will feel snappy or overly rigid, then compare that hypothesis with actual playtesting. It must be relevant to the work. No artificial quizzes or compulsory theoretical detours. ### Principle 3 — Evidence beats plausible narration Each important statement is **verified**, **inferred**, **proposed**, or **unknown**. An installed test script is not a passing test. A green test is not a successful manual playthrough. A model's fabricated “Human approved” field does not authorize anything. Agent handoffs start from the project's files and check Git/worktree state where possible. Chat history is useful context but insufficient authority for a stale plan. ### Principle 4 — One playable slice at a time A *slice* is a narrow, observable player experience. A full level, inventory, skill tree and save system in Sprint 001 would hide risks and make evaluation harder. Isolate the smallest experiment that tests the central unknown. Ideas not needed now stay in `planning/BACKLOG.md`; they are not lost, nor automatically approved. ### Principle 5 — Safety isn't an optional advanced feature The simple workflow retains three separate human gates: design, exact implementation authorization, and actual acceptance. Permission to run a terminal is not permission to run an arbitrary command. Permission to edit one file does not authorize a new package, API, deletion, deployment or network transfer. The validator checks **internal file consistency** but cannot authenticate consent. This limitation is intentional and documented. ### Principle 6 — Progressive disclosure The normal path needs six persistent Markdown files and, when work is chosen, `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, `REVIEW.md`. Add architecture diagrams, asset licensing inventories, release records or cross-sprint risk logs **only when needed**. A comprehensive wiki, generated manual and provider-specific skills can exist without burdening the user with all of them during onboarding. ### Example: avoiding false autonomy A student says: “Make enemy AI.” The agent asks which behavior should be observable in the first playtest, compares patrol-and-chase versus a stationary defender, and asks the student to choose. It writes acceptance criteria, then a narrow implementation plan. When the student says “I choose patrol,” the agent records Gate D **but does not code** until Gate I. Once the code is built, the student tries it and reports whether the chase is legible; the model does not award itself Gate A. ### Common failures **Process theater:** Files are complete but nobody tested the mechanic. Recover by defining observable acceptance criteria. **Agent overreach:** An adapter enables shell tools and assumes it may edit anything. Recover by checking the actual `PLAN.md` revision. **Documentation overload:** A novice gets nine questionnaires. Recover with the first-session script and a default `unknown` value. ### Related [Overview](#wiki-foundations--overview) · [Decision making](#wiki-learning--decisions) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Human playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting)

title: ADDF Light Games vs. Original ADDF
body: ## ADDF Light Games vs. Original ADDF This comparison is a **conceptual comparison of the current original ADDF v3.5 framework and the ADDF Light Games branch**, not a suggestion to overwrite or automatically merge them. The original repository's `main` branch remains the canonical full ADDF edition. ### When to use Consult this before choosing a methodology, explaining the game-focused adaptation, adopting Light in an existing full-ADDF project, or deciding whether to add more governance. ### Side-by-side comparison | Dimension | Original ADDF (v3.5) | ADDF Light Games | | --- | --- | --- | | **Primary domain** | General LLM-assisted software development | Games and interactive playable experiences | | **Intended user** | Operators comfortable with a detailed, auditable engineering process | Solo makers, students, designers and small game teams seeking low-friction guidance | | **Design goal** | Formal file-backed control across complex lifecycle and work scale | Preserve control while minimizing the *user's* process burden | | **Public lifecycle** | Eight steps: Research; Design & Feasibility; Validation Gate; Architecture; Sprint Planning; Build & Test; Review & Reflection; Deploy/Maintain/Resume | Five stages: Research; Design/Ideation; Implement; Refine; Acceptance | | **Operating boundaries** | Explicit Research Mode, Design Mode, Develop Mode | Same three distinct *capabilities*, with five player-facing lifecycle stages | | **Sprint workflow** | Eleven-step controlled Sprint Loop, including dry run and several human checks | One bounded iteration with three human gates, plus scope-aware refinement | | **Default project memory** | `AGENTS.md`, `DOMAIN.md`, `STATE.md`, `COMMANDS.md`, `SECURITY.md` and additional decision/question/risk/style files | Six persistent files: `AGENTS.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `GAME.md`, `STATE.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `planning/BACKLOG.md` | | **Game intent** | General domain is documented in `DOMAIN.md` | Player experience, core loop, design pillars and playable hypothesis in `GAME.md` | | **Sprint documents** | Typically separate `requirements.md`, `blueprint.md`, `acceptance.md`, `dry_run.md`, implementation log, human review and retrospective | Three files: `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, `REVIEW.md` | | **Research handling** | Dedicated research files, questions and risk tracking | Focused active sprint research; larger studies are optional | | **Human design control** | Explicit validation/blueprint and design review | **Gate D** for consequential direction and acceptance criteria | | **Code authorization** | Develop Mode starts with Permission Level 0 dry run and specific human authorization | **Gate I**, tied to exact plan revision, paths, commands, dependencies and side effects | | **Outcome acceptance** | Human review, approval and retrospective within sprint governance | **Gate A**, requiring actual human gameplay/review; tests alone do not count | | **Permission detail** | Formal Develop Mode permission levels and scale model | Core safe boundaries plus separate special approvals; advanced controls optional | | **Onboarding** | Copy full blank starter kit and initialize more project-memory files | Copy six files or adopt an existing repo read-only; choose first sprint later | | **User questioning** | Formal research/design workflows | Guided discovery: one consequential question at a time by default | | **Learning focus** | Engineering rigor, repeatability and auditability | Those goals **plus explicit game-design learning and playtest predictions** | | **Example deliverable** | General mini-task-tracker example and engineering artifacts | Dependency-free browser Duck Dodge pilot with real tests, plus onboarding/adoption exercises | | **Model integrations** | Model-agnostic prompt catalog | Nine lifecycle prompts and optional Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw skill adapters | | **Automated validation** | Full-ADDF checklists and governance procedures | Python structural validator and branch-only CI; warns that human consent cannot be authenticated | | **Documentation depth** | Extensive wiki and long consolidated reference | Extensive dedicated wiki and generated single-document manual, **without forcing every chapter into normal workflow** | | **Suitable scale** | Broad work, multi-team delivery, governance-heavy/high-risk projects | Prototypes, learning, smaller game projects and bounded playable feature increments | | **Relationship** | Independent canonical edition on `main` | Separate branch `ADDF_light_games`; **not** an automatic merge or replacement | Original ADDF itself is adaptable to work scale. It is inaccurate to say it *always* requires every optional file for the smallest patch. The distinction here is that Light **codifies** a tiny default runtime around game-playable evidence. ### What is deliberately preserved? Both editions require durable project memory, role-aware write boundaries, a dry-run before changing implementation, explicit human authorization, honest test evidence and resumable handoffs. Light is **not a permissionless mode**. ### What is deliberately reduced? Light consolidates sprint artifacts and keeps optional risk, architecture, asset, feature and release records out of the first-time template. Rather than a complete project brief, it can start from one sentence and expand only after decisions are made. That consolidation is a *navigation decision*, not permission to omit scope, source provenance, rollback, review history or security constraints. ### Choosing an edition Use **Light Games** if the immediate goal is to explore and validate playable behavior with a small team, to teach game mechanic/system/level design, or to build an incremental game prototype. Choose **original ADDF** when delivery requires detailed formal architecture, richer cross-team release governance, multiple risk tracks, or explicitly managed permission tiers. A real existing project can migrate only via an **audited, human-approved mapping**; do not blindly rename its `DOMAIN.md` to `GAME.md` or delete historic sprint records. ### References and verification Original ADDF evidence: [main README](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/main/README.md), [original lifecycle](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/main/docs/lifecycle/index.md), [original sprint loop](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/main/docs/sprint-loop.md), [original starter kit](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/main/starter-kit/README.md). Light contracts: [framework specification](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/FRAMEWORK_SPEC.md), [architecture](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/REPOSITORY_ARCHITECTURE.md), [sprint file contracts](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/SPRINT_FILE_CONTRACTS.md). ### Related [File reference](#wiki-reference--file-reference) · [Existing-project adoption](#wiki-guides--existing-project) · [Philosophy](#wiki-foundations--philosophy)

title: Core Concepts and How They Fit Together
body: ## Core Concepts and How They Fit Together ADDF Light Games consists of five interlocking concepts: **the game project**, **persistent project brain**, **bounded sprint**, **write capability**, and **human gate**. Confusing any pair of these is a common source of AI overreach. ### When to use Use this when an agent seems to conflate an approved design with implementation permission, a branch with a sprint, or a technical test with actual human acceptance. ### Project and framework are different things The framework distribution supplies rules and starter files. The individual game's project repository contains the actual source, game intent, current state and real approval records. The framework's `spec/` files are authoritative for distribution templates, but a game's current human-approved `GAME.md` and decisions reflect the user's project-specific intentions. The game engine is not the framework. A browser Canvas prototype, Phaser game, Godot project or Unity game may all follow the same decision and approval process. ### Project brain Six persistent files exist in a blank project: `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GAME.md`, `STATE.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `planning/BACKLOG.md`. They are intentionally small at first. The agent updates them as facts and choices become known. `STATE.md` is a **summary view**, not independent proof of human permission. The exact consent source and plan revision must be recoverable from the relevant sprint record. ### Sprint pack One sprint has three files under `planning/sprints/sprint-NNN/`: | File | Owns | Approval | | --- | --- | --- | | `SPRINT.md` | Goal, research, scope, design alternatives, learning checkpoint, `AC-##` criteria | Gate D | | `PLAN.md` | Exact file operations, dependencies, commands, risks, test plan, implementation record | Gate I | | `REVIEW.md` | Actual test outcomes, human observations, refinements, final verdict | Gate A | A sprint represents a bounded, verifiable **learning or playable outcome**. A backlog item is only a candidate, not an approved sprint. Creating a Git branch is not a substitute for creating/approving the sprint documents. ### Stages versus capabilities **Stages** communicate what work the person and agent are doing: research, design, implement, refine, accept. **Capabilities** govern file writes: - Research: safe investigation and notes, no source changes. - Design: project-brain and plan drafting, no source changes. - Develop: changes only inside a human-approved exact `PLAN.md`. An agent in the “Refine” stage may still need Develop capability and a valid Gate I to change code. ### Approval versus evidence A successful Node test establishes a particular behavior in a known execution environment. It does not show that a person liked the control feel. A line in `PLAN.md` saying `gate_i_status: authorized` must be linked to a real human response; the Python validator can check internal coherence **but cannot authenticate authorship**. A materially changed plan **invalidates** authorization tied to the older revision. Preserve the historical approval rather than overwriting it. ### Example: moving a duck The backlog holds “Make movement responsive.” Sprint 001 narrows it to four-direction movement in a small arena. A design choice considers acceleration, Gate D records the selected feel. The plan lists an exact JavaScript file, test command and no dependencies. Gate I permits that revision only. The agent implements, verifies directional movement and presents a runnable game. The human tests and provides Gate A. If the agent discovers a need for a new input package after starting, it **stops** and revises the plan instead of interpreting the initial authorization broadly. ### Common failures **Status as authority:** `STATE.md` says authorized but no consent source exists. Fail closed. **Overgrown sprint:** A sprint bundles several untested systems. Split into testable slices. **Lost evidence:** The agent stores all choices in chat only. Update `DECISIONS.md` and the sprint pack. ### Related [Lifecycle overview](#wiki-lifecycle--index) · [File reference](#wiki-reference--file-reference) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals)

title: Glossary
body: ## Glossary A concise shared vocabulary matters because an AI can otherwise treat “approve,” “test,” or “sprint” too loosely. ### When to use Use this when a term in a prompt, review, agent handoff, or validator report is unclear. | Term | Meaning in ADDF Light Games | | --- | --- | | **Acceptance criteria (`AC-##`)** | Observable checks written **before implementation**; each must have a corresponding `REVIEW.md` result | | **Agent / assistant** | An AI providing research, drafting or authorized implementation; it does not become the human project owner | | **Backlog (`B-###`)** | Future candidate outcomes and experiments, not implementation authorization | | **Capability** | Research, Design, or Develop write boundary; separate from the five lifecycle stages | | **Decision (`D-###`)** | Consequential human choice, including alternatives, rationale and future revisit trigger | | **Dry run** | Proposed exact file operations, commands, dependencies, risks and tests in `PLAN.md`, performed **without code edits** | | **Evidence** | Source, actual test result, inspectable artifact or human observation; classified as verified/inferred/proposed/unknown | | **Gate D** | Human decides material design direction and relevant sprint acceptance goal | | **Gate I** | Human explicitly authorizes a **specific current plan revision and scope**, before source edits | | **Gate A** | Human evaluates the actual outcome via first-hand test/review and supplies acceptance verdict | | **Human owner** | Person who approves significant design, authorization and acceptance; may delegate routine within-scope work | | **Light** | Low-friction daily use with thorough reference docs, not reduced safety or a light-color variant | | **Learning checkpoint** | A short explanation/prediction tied to a design tradeoff and later observation | | **Material scope change** | New paths, commands, dependency, risk, external effect or meaningful behavior; requires a revised Gate I | | **Optional module** | Advanced architecture, risk, feature/release or asset tracking added only when necessary | | **Plan revision (`rN`)** | Version of the technical authorization scope; old consent does not cover a materially changed revision | | **Playable slice** | Small, observable player action and game response that can be evaluated in one bounded iteration | | **Project brain** | Six persistent Markdown files recording safe rules, game intent, decisions, state and backlog | | **Refinement round (`round-N`)** | Preserved record of feedback, correction, retest and verdict in `REVIEW.md` | | **Research spike** | Bounded investigation with a specific evidence deliverable, not an automatically playable feature | | **Sprint** | One bounded game outcome or focused research experiment, with `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, `REVIEW.md` once active | | **Stage** | User-facing Research, Design/Ideation, Implement, Refine, Acceptance | | **State/status** | Current operational position in `STATE.md`; status must match the stage and actual gate evidence | | **Synthetic fixture** | Invented test data, which does not constitute a real person's approval or playtest | | **T0 / T1 / T2** | Routine detail / consequential design choice / high-impact safety or cost decision | | **Worktree** | Actual source-control checkout and uncommitted state; must be inspected before risky edits | ### Applying terms correctly “Design approved” means Gate D, not permission to write source. “Plan authorized” means Gate I for exactly one revision/scope, not permission to deploy. “Automated test passed” is evidence, not Gate A. “Accepted with conditions” preserves those conditions and cannot silently become an unconditional release. ### Common failures **Generic yes:** The human says “yes” but the agent cannot identify which revision and scope was displayed. Keep Gate I pending and ask a precise question. **Invented test:** A model narrates “I opened the game” without tool evidence or the person's report. Mark unverified. **Conflicting state:** The plan shows r2, the state refers to r1. Stop and reconcile. ### Related [Workflow states](#wiki-lifecycle--index) · [Approval policy](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Validator](#wiki-quality--validation)

title: Install the Minimal Starter Kit
body: ## Install the Minimal Starter Kit ADDF Light Games has no obligatory CLI installer. Installation means copying **six Markdown files into a new game-project folder**, then using a prompt to begin guided discovery. ### When to use Use this for a **new** project. If you already have code or a root `AGENTS.md`, follow [existing-project adoption](#wiki-guides--existing-project) instead; do not overwrite it. ### Before you begin You need a folder where you can create files and an AI assistant. You do **not** need Unity, Godot, Phaser, OpenClaw, a credit card, cloud hosting or a complete concept to start. Confirm you are viewing the `ADDF_light_games` branch of the framework, not the original `main`. The inherited `starter-kit/blank/` directory belongs to **full ADDF**. Light's six files live under `starter-kit/minimal/`. ### Copy these files ```text your-game/ ├── AGENTS.md ├── SECURITY.md ├── GAME.md ├── STATE.md ├── DECISIONS.md └── planning/ └── BACKLOG.md ``` Source: [Light starter kit](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/starter-kit/LIGHT_GAMES.md) and [minimal folder](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/tree/ADDF_light_games/starter-kit/minimal). The initial `STATE.md` reads `lifecycle_stage: research`, `sprint_status: discovering`, `active_sprint: none`, `authorized: no`. That's correct. The game title, engine and prototype goal may be `unknown`. **Do not copy the three sprint files yet.** They remain distribution templates under `starter-kit/sprint-template/` until the human chooses the first milestone. ### Initial verification 1. Open `SECURITY.md` and make sure its excluded paths and network restrictions fit your environment. Never add real secret values to the document. 2. Open `AGENTS.md`; it must describe Gate D, Gate I and Gate A and the roles' write boundaries. 3. Open `STATE.md`; confirm no implementation has been authorized. 4. Make sure `GAME.md` still labels unselected ideas as unknown, rather than falsely chosen. 5. Optionally run the Python validator after Stage 6 if you have Python installed: ```bash python3 /path/to/framework/scripts/validate_light.py /path/to/your-game ``` This is a **read-only** structural check. It is not a permission grant and cannot prove human consent. ### Optional integrations Claude Code can load a project skill under `.claude/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md`; Codex can load one under `.agents/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md`; OpenClaw is optional and requires its own deliberately configured workspace. Install these **only if you use that host**. The core six files are sufficient for manual chat workflows. ### Example: first few minutes The user says, “I want a small browser game but don't know what kind.” The agent reads safe project context and offers a dodge, path-puzzle or tactical encounter concept. The user selects one. The agent drafts a small player-facing goal, not game code. After the human chooses a milestone, it creates the sprint triplet and requests the two appropriate approvals. ### Common failures **Wrong source:** Copying the framework's root `AGENTS.md` or original full kit. Copy only the six Light `minimal/` files. **Premature paperwork:** Filling out a future Sprint 001 with fabricated decisions before the user has chosen anything. Leave it absent. **Unsafe existing repo:** Overwriting another project's instructions. Run the read-only adoption audit first. ### Related [First session](#wiki-guides--first-session) · [Quick reference](#wiki-guides--quick-reference) · [Existing-project adoption](#wiki-guides--existing-project)

title: Your First ADDF Light Games Session
body: ## Your First ADDF Light Games Session The first session should feel like a short game-design conversation, **not a form**. A user may start with no idea; the agent must provide useful choices without demanding a novel-length GDD. ### When to use Use this after copying the six starter files, or when showing a new game-design student how to ask an AI assistant for thoughtful help instead of one-shot generation. ### Before the conversation The agent reads `SECURITY.md` first, then `AGENTS.md` and `STATE.md`. It may read `GAME.md`, `DECISIONS.md` and the backlog when necessary. If it has no file access, the user can provide safe excerpts, and the agent must label its edits **proposed** instead of claiming it saved them. Never provide API keys, private accounts or hidden credentials to get the session started. ### The first prompt > Use ADDF Light Games. Read the project's SECURITY.md, AGENTS.md and STATE.md before exploring other files. Help me find **one small playable outcome** by asking one meaningful question at a time. Explain major design tradeoffs, label assumptions, and maintain the project brain if permitted. Do not edit game code, install packages or publish anything. Stop before implementation and show me an exact plan for my approval. Then add your idea—or simply say, “I have no idea what to make.” ### Session sequence 1. **Orient:** Establish whether the user has no idea, one sentence or an existing game. Report known versus inferred details. 2. **Discover:** Offer two or three genuinely distinct small ideas when needed. Each should have a player action, a system response and a feasible first slice. 3. **Learn:** Compare one consequential tradeoff such as instant movement versus acceleration, or a fixed obstacle versus a moving one. 4. **Choose:** Let the person select or defer. Record real decisions in `DECISIONS.md`; unanswered questions remain pending. 5. **Propose a sprint:** One observable goal, in/out scope, testing method and minimal risk. Move extra ideas to the backlog. 6. **Gate D:** Obtain an actual human decision on significant game direction and acceptance criteria. 7. **Prepare a dry run:** Draft `PLAN.md` with exact paths, commands, dependencies, risk and rollback. 8. **Gate I:** Stop and ask the human to authorize the actual plan revision. Only after explicit authorization may implementation begin. 9. **Gate A later:** The human plays the resulting game; automated test success is not acceptance. For most first sessions, stopping after steps 1–6 is perfectly useful. ### What the agent writes The agent updates `GAME.md` only for actual intended experience or clearly proposed ideas, allocates `D-###` entries for significant choices, and puts future candidates in `planning/BACKLOG.md`. Only after selecting an actual milestone does it create `planning/sprints/sprint-001/` from the three template files. It can draft technical assumptions and tests, but it cannot invent a past consent record. ### Example conversation **User:** “I want something about movement.” **Agent:** “Two small first slices: a duck avoiding horizontal obstacles, or a character jumping between two platforms. The first isolates movement clarity; the second adds timing and gravity. Which interaction do you want to study?” **User:** “Duck dodge, simple directional controls.” **Agent:** “We can start with immediate movement or acceleration. Immediate movement makes collision and responsiveness easier to evaluate; acceleration might feel more expressive but needs tuning. Which do you prefer?” **User:** “Immediate for Sprint 001.” That is a real design choice in the conversation. It is **not yet Gate I**. The agent should now show the exact first-sprint plan and ask permission before building. ### Closing the session Summarize last verified status, what documents changed, which gates are pending, and **one next action**. Update `STATE.md` if tools and permission allow. Next session begins with the [resumption protocol](#wiki-agents--handoff) rather than trusting a model's memory. ### Common failures **Too many questions:** Ask one impactful question, not ten unrelated preferences. **Overeager agent:** It generates the game immediately after the user selects a genre. Stop at the dry-run gate. **Pretend state:** A chat assistant claims it edited files without file tools. Provide a proposed diff instead. ### Related [No-idea route](#wiki-guides--from-zero) · [One-sentence route](#wiki-guides--from-idea) · [Design stage](#wiki-lifecycle--design) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals)

title: Starting Without a Game Idea
body: ## Starting Without a Game Idea “No idea yet” is an **acceptable and productive** initial state. Light's discovery protocol exists precisely so the human can learn and choose without having to supply an entire design brief. ### When to use Use this for new designers, a classroom warm-up, exploratory prototypes and users who know they want to make a game but cannot name a mechanic. ### Discovery procedure **Step 1 — Ask one preference, not a questionnaire.** For example: “Would you rather make something about movement, solving a puzzle, or tactical decisions—or should I suggest three options?” **Step 2 — Offer 2–3 differentiated concepts.** Each option should communicate: - the core player action; - what the system does in response; - the feeling or design principle it might explore; - one minimum playable experiment; - the main uncertainty. **Step 3 — Explain one design fork.** If the user chooses movement, compare direct versus momentum-based control. If they choose puzzles, compare open exploration versus a sequence of fixed challenges. The agent recommends a reversible starting experiment and says why. **Step 4 — Record the actual choice.** Update `GAME.md` and allocate a `D-###` record when the choice is consequential. If the user is unsure, mark the choice deferred and offer a small research spike. **Step 5 — Select the first slice.** Propose an observable milestone, such as “Move a placeholder in a visible arena and survive one obstacle.” Do not promise a complete scoring system, art style, levels, save system and multiplayer in one step. **Step 6 — Gate D then Gate I.** Significant design approval is recorded separately from permission to edit exact files. ### Worked example | Option | Player verb | Smallest playable slice | Primary learning | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Dodge the hazard | Move / avoid | One avatar, one repeating moving obstacle, collision and restart | Control feel and clarity | | Connect the path | Rotate / connect | Rotate tiles to join start and goal | Local feedback and puzzle legibility | | Two-unit tactics | Select / choose | Two controllable units and one visible conflict resolution | Rules, state and meaningful choice | A user picks the puzzle. The agent might ask: “Should a tile snap in quarter turns or rotate freely? Quarter turns are simpler and make valid connections unambiguous. Which first experiment should we build?” The user decides or asks for a side-by-side prototype. A good first `SPRINT.md` states only the chosen action, measurable outcome, in/out scope, learning objective and acceptance checks. A good `PLAN.md` names the exact files and commands needed to test that outcome. ### If the user cannot choose Do not force a direction or pretend an AI recommendation is a human decision. Offer a reversible 15-minute **design exercise** or focused no-code research. A formal code-producing prototype still requires an authorized sprint plan. ### What should not happen - No automatic engine selection based on the AI's comfort. - No full asset pipeline or monetization strategy before the player verb is known. - No prefilled “human approved” decision record. - No multi-page list of aesthetic preferences that delays the first useful test. ### Common failures **Options differ only in theme:** “Dodge asteroids,” “dodge cars,” “dodge fruit.” Offer different **interaction systems**, not merely art skins. **Unbounded ideation:** A hundred ideas without choosing. Limit to the smallest decision that unlocks a concrete sprint. **Agent chooses for the student:** The assistant may recommend, but must record the user's actual preference. ### Related [Guided discovery](#wiki-learning--guided-discovery) · [First session](#wiki-guides--first-session) · [Research](#wiki-lifecycle--research)

title: Starting With a One-Sentence Idea
body: ## Starting With a One-Sentence Idea An idea such as “a fishing game where the weather changes the fish” is enough to begin. The agent should **unpack it carefully**, not treat its guesses as settled facts or build an enormous project from it. ### When to use Use this when the user knows a fantasy, setting, core interaction or desired emotion but has not chosen the engine, control model, scope or technical system. ### Three-column understanding The first agent response distinguishes: | Category | Example for a weather-driven fishing game | | --- | --- | | **Known** | Fishing is the main activity; weather affects fish in some way | | **Inferred** | The player may cast a line; fish may have spawn rules; likely needs feedback | | **Unknown** | What weather changes; platform/input; arcade vs simulation; intended first slice | Do not convert inferred mechanics into `GAME.md` pillars without user confirmation. ### Narrow to a testable core Ask: “What should the player be able to do in the first five minutes of testing?” A useful slice could be: **press a button to cast a line; a simple rain toggle changes the visible chance of a fish appearing**. This tests the weather-mechanic relationship with placeholder art and no inventory/economy. Explain alternatives that actually affect the experience. For example, “weather changes bite probability” versus “weather changes fish movement” asks for a different test and different technical plan. Put boats, characters, maps, online co-op and nuanced ecosystems into the backlog until relevant. ### Research when needed If a claim about a target game engine or platform might change feasibility, check current authoritative documentation or perform a small bounded experiment. Record sources and unknowns. Never fabricate an engine feature, benchmark or API call. If the idea needs expensive hardware, credentials, a data source or paid service, propose an offline substitute for the first slice or request the necessary separate authorization. ### Write the design record The agent should maintain: - `GAME.md` — confirmed player action, intended experience, constraints and playable hypothesis; - `DECISIONS.md` — meaningful human selection among weather-mechanic alternatives; - `planning/BACKLOG.md` — deferred features; - `SPRINT.md` — one selected outcome, in/out scope and `AC-##` checks. Then prepare `PLAN.md` with exact implementation operations and seek Gate I. Do not preinstall dependencies while “doing research.” ### Example acceptance criteria **AC-01:** The player can initiate a cast with a clearly labeled input; the game shows the action. **AC-02:** Toggling rain changes the observed in-game indicator and affects one defined fishing rule. **AC-03:** Reset returns weather and fishing state to the chosen baseline. The criteria should specify methods, environment and evidence when actual sprint documents are written. A player must test whether the relation is understandable even if deterministic unit checks pass. ### Common failures **Scope inflation:** AI adds crafting, inventory and fishing economy. Recover by isolating one observable cause/effect. **False consensus:** It assumes realism, difficulty or graphics without user choice. Mark such matters unknown. **Early technology lock-in:** “Fishing implies Unity.” The framework is engine-agnostic; choose tools based on the actual slice. ### Related [Design](#wiki-lifecycle--design) · [Sprint planning](#wiki-sprints--planning) · [Backlog](#wiki-sprints--backlog)

title: Adopt Light in an Existing Game Project
body: ## Adopt Light in an Existing Game Project An existing repo has history, human-owned design choices, source files, build constraints and possibly an `AGENTS.md` that defines permissions. Light should **integrate** with that reality, not overwrite it. ### When to use Use this for an ongoing Phaser, Unity, Godot, Unreal, web or custom-engine project; for a repo previously using original ADDF; or for a classroom project with established files. ### Phase 1 — Read-only audit Before opening arbitrary files, identify likely secret paths and excluded data. Read relevant safe files and list: - engine/language and **verified** project structure; - existing design intent and gameplay systems; - run/build/test commands, distinguishing actual execution from documentation; - `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` or other project instructions that might conflict; - current branch/worktree, uncommitted work and important backups; - active issues, risks and unknowns. Do not run installers, apply a starter kit, change Git settings, rename files or edit game source during the audit. ### Phase 2 — Map without erasing | Existing document | Possible Light destination | Treatment | | --- | --- | --- | | GDD, design brief, README | `GAME.md` | Summarize confirmed intent; preserve original | | Existing agent instruction file | `AGENTS.md` | Review conflict; **never blindly overwrite** | | Roadmap or issue list | `planning/BACKLOG.md` | Map candidates with history | | Decisions and playtest notes | `DECISIONS.md` / `REVIEW.md` | Preserve actual sources and past verdicts | | Existing security policy | `SECURITY.md` | Retain stricter exclusions | | Prior full-ADDF sprint files | Light sprint triplet (optional migration) | Keep originals; map conceptual responsibilities | | Source/config/assets | Remain as-is | No adoption-time changes by default | The Stage 5 [existing-project fixture](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/examples/existing-project/README.md) illustrates an `AGENTS.md` conflict, a read-only audit and a proposal to **merge** instructions instead of replacing them. ### Phase 3 — Proposed migration plan Before a single adoption write, identify exact paths to create/modify/move/delete, what content would be copied or reinterpreted, impacts on existing rules, potential data loss, rollback and the branch/worktree where changes would occur. The human explicitly reviews that migration scope. General interest in Light does not authorize replacement of existing project instructions or code. Migrating project-brain documents is distinct from the Gate I needed for subsequent game implementation. ### Phase 4 — Safe initial state Once approved, create the minimal files where genuinely missing and record `project_origin: existing-project`. Start Light `STATE.md` in `research` / `discovering`, `authorized: no`, unless there is verifiable *current* Light sprint authorization. Existing code does not imply ongoing Gate I. Choose a modest first task: a reproducible bug, a new playtest, a single mechanic or a research spike. Draft the sprint pack only after the human selects it. ### Verify the adoption Compare the actual diff against the migration plan. Confirm old GDD, source, Git history and permissions remain accessible. If a file was overwritten accidentally, stop, preserve the diff and seek human instructions on restoring it. Do not force-reset uncommitted work. ### Common failures **Blind copy:** Overwriting a rich `AGENTS.md` with the Light template. Use a reviewed merge. **Fabricated test:** Assuming an existing project builds because a README contains a command. Mark not verified until run under proper permission. **Silent mode migration:** Converting original ADDF approval levels into new Gate I without checking whether consent still applies. Keep old records, re-approve current scope. ### Related [Install guide](#wiki-guides--install) · [Source-control safety](#wiki-quality--security) · [Original comparison](#wiki-foundations--comparison)
